posts.content:
the annual editorial calendar is dead and most teams havent noticed.

let me show show you what it looks like in 2026:

like any marketer i too built the big planning doc every january.

12 months of themes, mapped out, color coded, locked.

it felt "responsible"

honestly the only reason we ever did that was production was slow.

you needed lead time because writing everything from scratch took weeks.

so you planned far ahead to give the machine room to catch up.

fast forward to today.. AI gets you to a rough first draft in minutes.

the lead time bottleneck is just gone.

(the doc was never strategy, it was a workaround for being slow and i didnt want to admit that)

so you dont plan content in january anymore.

you plan it off whatever signal showed up this week.

a customer question, a competitor move, a thing your audience is actually arguing about right now.

content strategy isnt a doc you fill once every six months.

its a system that watches live signals and learns what lands.

you ship, you read the response, you adjust, you ship again.

this is the part i actually care about, because i wasted years treating the snapshot like it was the strategy.

maybe this is more a reflection for myself. but if you made it this far, stop filling the doc.

start building the loop.

posts.content:
most b2b founders treat their product launch like a "6-minute abs" workout.

a few weeks of hype, a multi-channel campaign, paid amplification, pr push, the works.

it doesn't work — and the math is brutal. the launch fails because the audience didn't exist beforehand, not because the campaign wasn't loud enough.

the founders i watch nail launches do the opposite:

> they spend 12–18 months publishing on linkedin before the product is even built

> when launch day comes, the entire campaign is one social post and one newsletter email

> the social post is from their personal account, not the brand

> the hook frames it as an announcement, the proof is specific, the visual is scrappy and human

> the link goes directly in the post — conversions beat marginal reach gains on launch day

> the CTA names what to do, specifically. "try it free" beats "check it out."

simple launch. years of work behind it. that's the actual play.

full breakdown in this week's newsletter.

posts.content:
most "why isn't my linkedin working" questions aren't a content problem.

they're a credibility problem.

the way i think about it:

performance = content best practices × credibility.

if either one is near zero, the output is near zero. you can have perfect hooks, perfect formatting, daily posts — and 50 impressions — because the market's silent question is still "why should i listen to you on this?"

what credibility actually is:

> years in the role you're selling to

> a track record your icp recognizes

> stories and specifics only a practitioner would have

> public reps that prove you've done the thing

if you have it, the answer to slow growth is mechanical: post more, talk in specifics, show up daily. you're on easy mode.

if you don't, your three honest options:

> build for a space where you already have credibility

> bring in someone who does and put them at the center of content

> post as a builder/learner — not a guru

skipping credibility isn't a tactic. there isn't one.

full breakdown in this week's newsletter.

honestly the most useful thing here is that last line. stop filling the doc, start building the loop. most content teams I know are very good at filling docs and have never once audited whether the loop is working.
The system has shifted from being static to an adaptive one. In the AI era, the new version of the content engine flow is likely to get more responses than the older one.
The teams that win will be the ones that can adapt quickly to real audience signals while maintaining a clear strategic direction.

We piloted a weekly signal review last quarter where the team spent 30 minutes on Mondays pulling what the audience was actually engaging with. Content volume dropped by about 20% but the stuff we shipped had a measurably higher response rate across every format we tracked.
This really resonates! Agility has become a bigger advantage than rigid planning. The teams winning today aren’t just planning better; they’re learning faster and adapting in real time.

I spent six months trying to get a leadership team to stop asking for the quarterly content plan and start trusting the weekly queue. The calendar wasn't just comfortable to them, it was how they felt included in the process. When you kill the doc you sometimes accidentally exclude the people who used it to stay connected.
I think about this every time someone tells me they're working on their "content strategy." Ask them to show you the loop and most of the time there isn't one. There's a folder with a plan in it.

My first content strategy job we had a beautiful annual calendar and I was so proud of it. The second month my manager asked why we weren't writing about a product thing that was obviously blowing up in the community and I didn't have a good answer. The calendar had themes. The theme wasn't that.

And there's a version of this that's still reactive in a bad way. "A competitor moved so we respond" can pull a team off its own positioning just as fast as a rigid calendar can. The difference between watching signals and chasing noise is the judgment layer in between, and that's where most teams actually fall apart.

Signal-first approach also reframes how you hire. You stop looking for someone who can execute a plan and start looking for someone who can read a room. Different skill set entirely and most job descriptions haven't caught up to that.

It reminds me of how film studios used to greenlight based on what worked in the last cycle. Not because it was smart but because the approval process was so slow you had to bet before the market moved. Then streaming collapsed that lag and suddenly nobody knew what they were doing. Same energy here.

I'll push on one thing. Shipping off live signals works great for established brands with enough audience to generate real signal. If you're early and small, you might not have enough feedback to read. What do you do before you have a real loop to learn from?
I still use a quarterly skeleton but what I put in it is different now. Channel, format, rough volume. No themes, no topics, nothing that assumes I know what my audience will care about in September.
Twelve months, twelve themes, color-coded. I built the same doc. Shipped from it maybe twice.

Two things can be true here though. The annual doc was covering for slow production, yes. But it was also doing real stakeholder alignment work. When you cut the doc you often cut the shared visibility. That part needs to replace itself somehow or you're just creating a different problem.

I ran demand gen at my last company for two years before I admitted our editorial calendar was just a way to look organized in all-hands. We shipped maybe 30% of what we planned and the stuff that actually moved pipeline came from things we decided on a Tuesday.
the "I didn't want to admit that" part is doing a lot of work in this post. most process problems stay in place because someone's self-image is attached to the process.

What I'm still figuring out is how to give a board or a CFO the signal-driven answer when they ask "what's your content plan for Q3." They don't want to hear "we're watching for signals." They want a document. Anyone cracked how to present this approach upward in a way that sticks?

I wasted years on the same snapshot mistake and I think part of it was that we kept celebrating the doc itself. Like finishing the January plan was an achievement. The ship and read and adjust loop has no finish line and that makes it harder to celebrate, which means you have to actually be bought in on the outcome.
Treated the snapshot like it was the strategy is going to stick with me. That's exactly what I spent most of my career doing and I had no framework to even notice it until it was already behind me.

We tested this in Q3 of last year. Cut the six-month plan down to a rolling four-week queue seeded from signal. Engagement went up 34% and our team stopped feeling like they were writing into the void.

Three years as an SDR building my personal outreach around a content calendar I thought made me look like a real marketer. I had scheduled posts about "thought leadership themes" while every good conversation I was having was about something totally different. Took switching jobs to figure out the doc was a comfort object.
Pulled from this one thing. Going to go through our current content plan this week and audit how much of it came from real signals versus what we assumed in January. My guess is the ratio is bad.
